comments.text:
My only problem with this review is 4K only.

I understand the comparison you're doing and that's fine, but the 4090 IMO is the first GPU ever that I would consider a 4K RT gaming GPU.  For any GPUs in the past you have to make multiple tweaks to settings for the GPU to be fast enough for 4K RT gaming.    So I find the 4090 to be in a class by itself and comparing anything to it makes those things look pathetic.

So, with the 4090 in a class by itself when it comes to being able to use RT in gaming, one can't expect 4K RT gaming in anything else and you're testing shows that, unless once again you make a lot of tweaks to quality settings.  So to me, the 4080 is a 2K RT gaming GPU and that's what I would have wanted to see benchmarked like what you did.  Leave most quality settings alone and then run this 2K RT.  I'm sure that's where it's performance range is because it's certainly not 4K RT and PC gamers don't want to run a game with such low fps.

So I don't know what all this testing shows for a typical user, until the end where raster performance is compared.  At least there people get to see how 4K gaming is moving down the product stack.  After all, most people are going to have a 1080p, 2K or 4K monitor and that's it and they'll want to game at the resolution of the monitor now, with the exception of 4K where you can have a 4K monitor and game at 1080p since the math works well, where 4 pixels become like a single pixel and you don't lose any image quality from an unevenness of pixels in horizontal vs. vertical in going from 4K to 1080p.

To me this DOES look like a GPU that I can use for either high quality 2K RT gaming, but I'm having to do some guessing, or I can using with a 4K monitor and run non RT @4K or RT @1080p on that 4K monitor.  So either way it's a win.  Pricing is still the issue, but using it with either a 2K or 4K monitor looks feasible.

If you want the smallest transistors, you'll be paying a premium now, no matter if you are NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel. You can already see it in smartphones, where the latest snapdragon with the latest node can add over $100 to the cost, all else being equal, compared to a lesser chip from a slightly older fabrication. Now extrapolate that to a giant GPU. I honestly don't see what much of the fuss is about. You can already hit 4k60 with last gen cards and turn on DLSS and RT and still hit even higher framerates. It feels like a pure numbers game at this point. My card can't break 500fps in counterstrike or some such nonsense. You can't see or appreciate any of it anyway. I think it's disingenuous to compare price between SKUs and say that the pricing is unfair. What should be done instead is to determine performance per dollar, and then plot them on a dot graph. comments.text: Although it's kept being referred to as "being held back by the CPU", it may be that the margin between the 4080 and 4090 didn't totally materialise because of game engine bottleneck. Many of these games that provide high graphic fidelity may not actually be designed to run at frame rate of an e-sport title. With the 40 series card, we are often seeing frame rate beyond 100 FPS, and we are seeing the percentage delta between 4080 and 4090 being much wider when the game is "forced" (highest RT settings without using DLSS) to run at a "lower" frame rate (like in the 70s to 90s). Put simply, these cards are just too powerful for the engines that prioritise graphic fidelity. The 4090 has 70% more compute performance in terms of raw flops, so you have got to think why we are not seeing that 70% extra performance. Of course, the usual explanation is "bottlenecked by something", but perhaps that "something" may just be the game engines that current titles are running on?
